```{r decisions-setup, include=FALSE}
has_gmp <- requireNamespace("gmp", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_gmp, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
options(width = 90)
```

A multidomain report card assigns each unit one integer grade in each domain:
Grade 1 is the highest priority within that domain, and giving two units the
same grade leaves that pair unordered without claiming that their targets are
equal. This article explains when each domain's grade column can be chosen on
its own and when a joint cross-domain protection rule changes the chosen
profile. All executable examples use small synthetic distributions, run offline
without an external MIP or LP solver, and evaluate exact fractions when the
suggested `gmp` package (`install.packages("gmp")`) is installed.

```{r decisions-load, eval=TRUE}
library(postrank)
```

```{r decisions-dependency-note, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=TRUE}
if (!has_gmp) cat("**Computation skipped:** the optional package `gmp` is not installed. Install `gmp` and rebuild to run the examples.\n")
```

## Additive domain loss and separate column choices

Let $G_d$ be the integer grade column in domain $d$, $F_d$ the number of
wrong-direction ordered pairs in a posterior state (counting any strict ordering
of equal targets as wrong), and $T_d$ the number of unordered (`withheld`) pairs
among all $M = \binom{n}{2}$ original unit pairs. With nonnegative domain
weights $w_d$ and unordered-pair costs $\tau_d$, the additive posterior expected
loss is

\[
R(G) = \sum_d w_d \frac{\mathbb{E}[F_d] + \tau_d T_d}{M}.
\]

Each domain's loss term depends only on within-domain pairwise probabilities.
Whenever the declared candidate set is a Cartesian product of per-domain column
sets and every constraint is within-domain (such as `equality_classes`, grade
caps, or per-domain expected-error budgets `q`), the feasible set is also a
Cartesian product: minimizing each weighted domain term on its own minimizes
$R(G)$ regardless of how domains depend on one another in the posterior (for a
zero-weight domain, every feasible column achieves zero weighted contribution).

Adding a **joint exceedance cap** across domains couples the feasible set. Writing
$N_d$ for the number of ordered pairs in domain $d$'s protection scope, a joint
cap requires

\[
J(G) = \Pr(\text{at least one } d \text{ has } F_d > t_d N_d) \le \alpha.
\]

Because this union event is evaluated inside each **joint posterior state**,
changing how errors co-occur across domains can change $J(G)$ while leaving
every marginal domain error probability and $R(G)$ unchanged (when $N_d = 0$,
$F_d > t_d N_d$ cannot occur in domain $d$, and that domain's error proportion
is `NA` rather than a measured zero).

## Two units, two domains, and identical marginal errors

Consider two units (`A` and `B`) across two domains (`one` and `two`). In a
normal state, `A` is above `B` (`2 > 1`); in a reversed state, `B` is above `A`
(`1 < 2`). The two discrete distributions below have identical marginal reversal
probability `1/10` in each domain, differing only in whether reversals happen
together or in separate states:

| Distribution | Normal in both | Reverse domain `one` only | Reverse domain `two` only | Reverse both |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `coincident` | `9/10` | `0` | `0` | `1/10` |
| `disjoint` | `8/10` | `1/10` | `1/10` | `0` |

We set equal domain weights (`1/2` each by default), unordered-pair cost
`tau = "1/4"`, strict error-proportion threshold `t = "0"`, and joint exceedance
cap `alpha = "3/20"` using character strings so exact rational values are kept:

```{r decisions-targets}
units <- c("A", "B")
domains <- c("one", "two")
targets <- setNames(lapply(domains, function(d) list(
  definition = paste("Fictional priority in domain", d),
  units = "arbitrary priority units", orientation = "larger_is_higher",
  equality_classes = units,
  equality_provenance = "A and B are distinct modeled targets."
)), domains)

make_states <- function(reverse, ids) {
  x <- array(0, c(nrow(reverse), 2L, 2L), dimnames = list(ids, units, domains))
  for (d in seq_along(domains)) {
    x[, "A", d] <- ifelse(reverse[, d], 1, 2)
    x[, "B", d] <- ifelse(reverse[, d], 2, 1)
  }
  x
}
```

```{r decisions-laws}
make_law <- function(id, reverse, masses) {
  postrank_mdomain_input(
    make_states(reverse, paste0(id, "-", seq_len(nrow(reverse)))),
    targets = targets,
    provenance = list(
      input_id = id, law_id = id, proper_law = TRUE,
      joint_generation = "Complete finite support authored in this article.",
      sampling_assumptions = list(
        finite_support_origin = "All support states and exact masses listed here.")
    ),
    representation = "exact_finite_law", masses = masses)
}
laws <- list(
  coincident = make_law("coincident",
    rbind(c(FALSE, FALSE), c(TRUE, TRUE)), c("9/10", "1/10")),
  disjoint = make_law("disjoint",
    rbind(c(FALSE, FALSE), c(TRUE, FALSE), c(FALSE, TRUE)),
    c("8/10", "1/10", "1/10"))
)
policy <- postrank_mdomain_decision(tau = "1/4", t = "0", alpha = "3/20")
```

With two units, each domain has three possible grade columns: `withhold`
(`1, 1`), `A_above_B` (`1, 2`), and `B_above_A` (`2, 1`). Their Cartesian
product contains all nine two-domain cards (`max_actions = 9L`). **Optimality in
`postrank_mdomain_solve()` holds within the declared candidate set** (which here
exhausts all two-unit profiles):

```{r decisions-solve-bank}
columns <- list(withhold = c(A = 1L, B = 1L),
  A_above_B = c(A = 1L, B = 2L), B_above_A = c(A = 2L, B = 1L))
families <- lapply(laws, postrank_mdomain_family,
  columns = list(one = columns, two = columns), max_actions = 9L)
fits <- setNames(lapply(names(laws), function(id) {
  postrank_mdomain_solve(laws[[id]], families[[id]], policy, max_actions = 9L)
}), names(laws))
```

```{r decisions-candidate-tables}
column_label <- function(g) {
  if (g[1L] == g[2L]) "withhold" else if (g[1L] < g[2L]) "A above B" else "B above A"
}
candidate_display <- function(fit) {
  tab <- fit[["candidate_table"]]
  actions <- fit[["solution"]][["actions"]][tab[["action_id"]]]
  data.frame(
    one = vapply(actions, function(g) column_label(g[, "one"]), ""),
    two = vapply(actions, function(g) column_label(g[, "two"]), ""),
    risk = tab[["risk_exact"]], joint_probability = tab[["J_exact"]],
    feasible = tab[["feasible_for_represented_measure"]],
    optimal = tab[["optimal"]], row.names = NULL
  )
}
knitr::kable(candidate_display(fits[["coincident"]]),
  caption = "All nine candidates: coincident reversals")
knitr::kable(candidate_display(fits[["disjoint"]]),
  caption = "All nine candidates: disjoint reversals")
```

Reporting `A above B` in both domains has additive loss `1/10` under both
distributions, yet its joint exceedance probability `J` is `1/10` (`<= 3/20`,
feasible) under `coincident` and `1/5` (`> 3/20`, infeasible) under `disjoint`:

```{r decisions-fixed-dual}
dual <- matrix(c(1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), 2L, dimnames = list(units, domains))
dual_evaluations <- lapply(laws, postrank_mdomain_evaluate,
  grades = dual, decision = policy)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(laws), function(id) {
  e <- dual_evaluations[[id]]
  data.frame(law = id, error_one = e[["domain_table"]][["EF_exact"]][1L],
    error_two = e[["domain_table"]][["EF_exact"]][2L], risk = e[["risk_exact"]],
    joint_probability = e[["J_exact"]],
    feasible = e[["feasible_for_represented_measure"]])
})), caption = "The same dual card (A above B in both domains) under both joint laws")
```

Under `disjoint`, two cards tie for the minimum feasible loss
$(1/2)(1/10 + 1/4) = 7/40$ with joint exceedance probability `1/10`—reporting
`A above B` in one domain and leaving the other domain unordered:

```{r decisions-all-optima}
optima <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(id) {
  tab <- candidate_display(fits[[id]])
  data.frame(law = id, tab[tab[["optimal"]], ], row.names = NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(optima, caption = "All optimal feasible candidates in the declared sets")
```

Removing the joint exceedance cap (`t = NULL`) restores separate domain
optimization, making `(A above B, A above B)` optimal (`risk = 1/10`) under both
laws—confirming that the union constraint is what coupled the domains, and that
pairing separate marginal simulations arbitrarily cannot determine which joint
distribution applies:

```{r decisions-separable}
separable_policy <- postrank_mdomain_decision(tau = "1/4", t = NULL)
separate_fits <- setNames(lapply(names(laws), function(id) {
  postrank_mdomain_solve(laws[[id]], families[[id]], separable_policy, max_actions = 9L)
}), names(laws))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  law = names(laws),
  optimum_risk = vapply(separate_fits, function(f) f[["evaluation"]][["risk_exact"]], ""),
  optimizer_count = vapply(separate_fits, `[[`, 1L, "optimizer_count")
))
```

## Reading the stored 40-site synthetic illustration

The JSON file `extdata/mdomain/synthetic40-card.json` stores summary tables and
grade matrices for 40 synthetic sites adapted from JoonHo Lee's
[Need-Based Prekindergarten Funding tutorial](https://github.com/joonho112/need-based-prek-funding-tutorial).
Domain `S` measures student-composition economic need and domain `C` measures
catchment-community economic need (larger values mean higher priority in both
domains, with `M = 780` unordered site pairs). Two site pairs (`S05`/`S06` and
`S21`/`S22`) share community `C` equality classes while all 40 student `S`
targets remain distinct (including conditional predictive `S` targets for new
sites).

In the external tutorial workflow, candidate selection used `8,000` post-warmup
states from chains `1–2` across a declared `7 x 7 = 49` candidate set (with
candidate columns ordered on those selection states), followed by fixed-card
evaluation on `8,000` states from chains `3–4`. Both cases use equal domain
weights, `tau = "1/10"`, `q = "1/20"`, and `alpha = "1/20"`, while `t` shifts
from `5%` (`primary`) to `10%` (`wide`).

**This article reads the stored grades and summary counts directly; it does not
rerun the 40-site selection, load the external posterior archive, or run a new
validation.** Full workflow details are in the tutorial's
[reproducibility appendix](https://github.com/joonho112/need-based-prek-funding-tutorial/blob/ff223082b27c8af92f762c20f49092f06b19a913/appendices/D-reproducibility.qmd)
(the source commit, relative path, SHA-256 hash, and adaptations are recorded in
the JSON file):

```{r decisions-stored-card, eval=TRUE}
stored <- jsonlite::read_json(system.file("extdata", "mdomain",
  "synthetic40-card.json", package = "postrank"), simplifyVector = TRUE)
knitr::kable(stored[["cases"]][, c("case_id", "t", "N_S", "N_C", "risk_exact",
  "selection_J_exact", "diagnostic_J_exact")],
  caption = "Stored 40-site summary counts (exact fractions over the 8,000-state empirical samples)")
```

- **`main-alpha-1_20` (`t = "1/20"`, or `5%`; grade columns `primary_S` and `primary_C`)**:
  leaves all `S` pairs unordered (`N_S = 0`) and orders `500` `C` pairs into
  three grades of sizes `10`, `10`, and `20`, with selection loss
  `170039/2496000`. Exceeding `5%` strictly across `500` ordered pairs requires
  at least `26` wrong-direction pairs (`25` does not exceed `5%`): `0` selection
  states reached `26` errors even though `1,871` states had at least one
  wrong-direction pair, so `J = 0` records zero threshold exceedances and does
  not claim an error-free ranking.
- **`sensitivity-t-wide` (`t = "1/10"`, or `10%`; grade columns `wide_S` and `wide_C`)**:
  orders `300` `S` pairs and `500` `C` pairs, with selection loss
  `716341/12480000`, selection exceedance rate `266/8000 = 133/4000`, and
  diagnostic-chain exceedance rate `229/8000`. **Exact fractions here represent
  exact arithmetic on the 8,000-state empirical samples; splitting MCMC chains
  does not make them independent or provide an IID numerical guarantee for the
  intended posterior.**

```{r decisions-stored-grades, eval=TRUE}
knitr::kable(stored[["grades"]],
  caption = "Stored 40-site grades (Grade 1 indicates highest priority in each domain)")
wide_grades <- as.matrix(stored[["grades"]][, c("wide_S", "wide_C")])
rownames(wide_grades) <- stored[["grades"]][["unit_id"]]
colnames(wide_grades) <- c("S", "C")
occupancy <- table(C = factor(wide_grades[, "C"], levels = 1:3),
                   S = factor(wide_grades[, "S"], levels = 1:2))
knitr::kable(occupancy, caption = "Wide card cell counts: rows are C grades, columns are S grades")
knitr::kable(wide_grades[c("S11", "S18"), , drop = FALSE],
  caption = "A crossed site pair: S11 has higher S priority, whereas S18 has higher C priority")
```

Across the six `(C, S)` profile cells, the row counts are `(6, 4)`, `(4, 6)`,
and `(0, 20)` (`5` of `6` cells occupied). Among the `548` site pairs ordered in
at least one domain, `16` pairs reverse priority across domains—such as
`S11 = (1, 2)` versus `S18 = (2, 1)`, where collapsing the two domains into one
ranking would require an extra policy choice.

*Data attribution:* `synthetic40-card.json` is adapted from JoonHo Lee (2026)
under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) (tutorial code
MIT licensed; source-specific exclusions remain in the tutorial's
[rights notice](https://github.com/joonho112/need-based-prek-funding-tutorial/blob/ff223082b27c8af92f762c20f49092f06b19a913/RIGHTS.md);
no raw posterior archives, geographic layers, or administrative school records
are bundled in `postrank`).

## Inspecting MCMC exceedance-event histories for a fixed multidomain card

To inspect how a Markov chain explores the exceedance event of a fixed report
card, pass `representation = "mcmc_equal_weight_draws"` with `state_origin` and
call `postrank_mdomain_assess(..., method = "mcmc")`. Below we simulate two
short unequal-length two-state Markov chains (`24` and `31` iterations,
transition probabilities `1/10` for `0 -> 1` and `2/5` for `1 -> 0`, stationary
reversal probability `1/5`; illustrative lengths only, independent of the
40-site file above):

```{r decisions-mcmc-sim}
simulate_chain <- function(n) {
  z <- logical(n)
  z[1L] <- stats::runif(1) < 1 / 5
  for (i in 2:n) {
    z[i] <- if (z[i - 1L]) stats::runif(1) >= 2 / 5 else stats::runif(1) < 1 / 10
  }
  z
}
set.seed(1202)
chains <- list(chain_A = simulate_chain(24L), chain_B = simulate_chain(31L))
z <- unlist(chains, use.names = FALSE)
history <- data.frame(
  source_index = seq_along(z),
  chain_id = rep(names(chains), lengths(chains)),
  iteration_id = unlist(lapply(chains, seq_along), use.names = FALSE)
)
```

Next we wrap the two-chain history in `postrank_mdomain_input()` and evaluate
`postrank_mdomain_assess(..., method = "mcmc", batch_size = 10L)` on the fixed
dual card `(A above B, A above B)`:

```{r decisions-mcmc-input}
history_input <- postrank_mdomain_input(
  make_states(cbind(z, z), paste0("markov-", seq_along(z))), targets = targets,
  provenance = list(
    input_id = "tiny-markov-history", law_id = "tiny-markov-law", proper_law = TRUE,
    joint_generation = "Both domains share the simulated binary chain state.",
    retention = list(warmup_removed = 0L, thinning = 1L),
    sampling_assumptions = list(
      sampler = "Two-state Markov transition simulator.",
      chain_details = "Lengths 24 and 31; stationary initial draws; seed 1202.",
      target_assertion = "Stationary reversal probability 1/5.")
  ),
  representation = "mcmc_equal_weight_draws", state_origin = history)
```

```{r decisions-mcmc-assess}
assessment <- postrank_mdomain_assess(history_input, dual, policy,
  method = "mcmc", batch_size = 10L,
  design = list(role = "synthetic_method_demonstration"))
chain_table <- assessment[["native"]][["chain_table"]]
knitr::kable(chain_table[chain_table[["event_id"]] == "joint-union",
  c("chain_id", "n_retained", "hit_count", "rate", "max_zero_run",
    "partial_batch_count")], digits = 3)
assessment[["assurance"]][c("certificate_basis", "numerical_guarantee",
  "convergence_established", "independence_established")]
```

Per-chain hit counts, `max_zero_run`, and batch-level tables
(`assessment$native$batch_table`, which keeps trailing partial batches rather
than dropping them) summarize how often the chain visited the exceedance event
(when combining chains of unequal length, weight by `n_retained` rather than
averaging unweighted chain rates). **MCMC diagnostics are descriptive summaries,
not guarantees:** they do not provide an IID binomial certificate, prove
convergence, or turn split chains into independent validation samples. See
`?postrank_mdomain_assess` for the fixed-sample `method = "iid"` design fields
and [Grading entities across multiple domains](mdomain-quickstart.html) for the
step-by-step multidomain workflow.
